facts.text: Before insulin was discovered, diabetes was often fatal, and children were especially at risk.
The diet promoted by Frederick Allen strictly limited carbohydrates and included repeated fasting. It added only about 2 to 3 months to patients’ lives.
Many patients abandoned the Allen diet, and the doctor Elliott Joslin compared it to starving a child so that he could stay alive.
In 1921 the Canadian surgeon Frederick Banting began work in John Macleod’s laboratory at the University of Toronto. Macleod was doubtful but gave him space and a student assistant, Charles Best.
Best was reportedly picked to be Banting’s assistant by tossing a coin.
On 30 July 1921 Banting and Best collected a liquid extract from the pancreas, which they first named Isletin.
Macleod was not convinced by their first results and asked for more tests, which confirmed them.
In December 1921 Macleod brought in the biochemist James Collip to make the extract purer.
On 11 January 1922 Leonard Thompson, a 14-year-old boy, received the first insulin injection at Toronto General Hospital. It failed: the dose was too small and he had an allergic reaction.
Collip improved the extract over the following 12 days, and Thompson’s second injection, on 23 January 1922, brought his blood sugar down sharply.
Thompson lived for 13 more years after the treatment.
Elizabeth Hughes, daughter of the U.S. Secretary of State Charles Hughes, arrived in Toronto on 15 August 1922 and began insulin treatment the next day.
At 14, Elizabeth Hughes was 5 feet tall, weighed 45 pounds, and could barely walk.
About three months after starting insulin, Hughes went home healthier, weighing more than twice as much as before, that is, more than 90 pounds.

Banting, Best, Collip and Macleod sold the insulin patent to the University of Toronto’s Connaught Laboratories for one dollar, a symbolic sum, partly to control quality and to stop any one company from controlling a life-saving drug.
Eli Lilly received sole rights for one year to manufacture insulin for sale, since producing it on a large scale required a major drug company.
The 1923 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine went to Banting and Macleod, who split their prize money with Best and Collip.
Insulin has saved millions of lives around the world.
Most people with type 1 diabetes must take insulin every day to control their blood sugar and stay alive, and they have the disease for the rest of their lives.
Insulin turned type 1 diabetes from a terminal illness into a manageable disease with close to normal life expectancy.
Banting hoped that insulin would be a drug people could afford.
In the United States, the price of a vial of Humalog, a modern insulin, rose from 21 dollars in 1999 to 332 dollars in 2019.
